What Actually Drives the Total Cost of a Time and Attendance System
A vendor quotes a per employee per month rate for time and attendance software, and that number becomes the anchor for the whole budget conversation. It’s clean, it’s easy to multiply by headcount, and it’s almost never the full cost a CFO or Ops leader ends up paying.


The subscription line covers the software layer, scheduling, exception handling, approvals, reporting, and the sync into payroll. It does not necessarily cover what happens at the point where an hourly employee actually clocks in. For any employer with an on-site workforce, that second layer, physical time clock hardware, its install, its device type, its maintenance, sits outside the software subscription and gets priced on its own terms. Growth-stage employers evaluating a system for the first time (or replacing a patchwork of spreadsheets and an aging punch clock) tend to discover this the hard way, midway through a vendor conversation, when “per employee per month” turns out to be the beginning of the quote, not the end of it.
Headcount and location count set the software baseline
The software subscription for a time and attendance platform scales primarily with two inputs: how many employees are being tracked and how many locations those employees work across. A single-site employer with 60 hourly staff has a fairly simple configuration. A 300-employee employer running four locations, each with its own manager, its own shift patterns, and its own approval chain, needs the platform to handle multi-location scheduling, role-based manager approvals, and consolidated reporting across sites. That complexity is what the recurring subscription is actually pricing, not just a headcount multiplier.


Most time and attendance vendors, Asure included, quote software pricing rather than publish a flat public rate, because the real cost driver is this combination of employee count, location count, and how much of the workflow (scheduling, exceptions, overtime rules, approvals) needs to be configured for the business. Two companies with the same headcount can land on very different quotes depending on how many locations and approval layers are involved.
Hardware enters the picture the moment punches happen on site
Software pricing covers the platform. It does not cover the physical device an employee uses to clock in, and that is where a second, separate cost structure begins. A remote or field-based workforce might clock in entirely through a mobile app, in which case hardware cost is close to zero. An on-site hourly workforce, in a warehouse, a clinic, a restaurant, a manufacturing floor, usually needs one or more physical time clocks per location, and the device type changes both the upfront cost and the ongoing considerations.


A basic badge or PIN clock is the simplest option. A fingerprint or touchless facial recognition clock adds a layer of accuracy against buddy punching and time theft, which matters more as headcount and location count grow, but it is also a different price point and a different install than a badge reader. The number of clocks per location, the punch method, and whether the business needs GPS-verified mobile punches for field employees alongside on-site devices all change the hardware line independently of the software subscription.


This is where the honest answer is to point to the source rather than guess at a number. Asure Time & Attendance runs the software layer, but the physical devices themselves come from PayClock, delivered through Lathem, an Asure company that has manufactured time and attendance hardware since 1919. For the specific devices, punch methods, and current lineup, the PayClock time clocks for PayClock Online page on Lathem’s site is the accurate source, since device pricing and specifications are Lathem’s to publish rather than something to estimate secondhand.
Integration and payroll sync change the calculation
The least visible cost driver is what happens between the time clock and the payroll run. If hours captured in the time and attendance system have to be manually exported, cleaned up, and re-entered into payroll, that gap shows up as staff hours, not as a line item on any invoice, and it compounds every pay period.


Asure Time & Attendance captures employee hours, manages exceptions and approvals, and syncs approved time directly into payroll without manual re-entry, and it does that inside AsureCentral, which connects time and attendance, scheduling, and payroll in one system so multi-location employers are not re-entering hourly workforce data across separate tools. For a controller evaluating total cost, that integration is worth pricing in explicitly. A cheaper system that requires a payroll administrator to spend two hours per pay cycle reconciling timecards by hand is not actually the cheaper system once that labor is accounted for.
Implementation and support carry a cost too
The person configuring a new time and attendance system is often an office manager or administrator juggling payroll alongside several other responsibilities, without a dedicated IT resource to lean on. Implementation time, training for managers who will approve exceptions, and the ongoing reliability of support when something breaks are all real costs, even when they don’t appear as a separate fee on the contract.


This is also where the difference between a low upfront quote and a workable long-term system tends to show up. A system that is hard to configure or comes with unreliable support creates ongoing labor cost long after the sale closes, in the form of manual corrections, disputed hours, and repeated calls to a help desk. Evaluating implementation and support quality alongside the subscription price is a necessary part of getting an accurate total cost picture.
Building a real total cost picture before signing
Pulling these threads together, the questions that actually determine what a time and attendance system will cost are:


* How many employees and locations does the software need to support, and how much scheduling and approval complexity comes with that footprint
* How many physical time clocks are needed, and does the workforce need badge, PIN, fingerprint, or touchless punch methods
* Does the system sync approved hours directly into payroll, or does someone need to re-enter them by hand each pay cycle
* What does implementation look like, and what is support like once the system is live


Working through these in order, rather than starting and stopping at the software subscription number, is the difference between a budget that holds and one that gets revised three months into the contract. For a step-by-step walkthrough of that evaluation and rollout process, How to Select and Implement Time and Attendance Software in Five Procedures for Growth-Stage Teams lays out the procedure end to end.
Where the software and hardware pieces come from in practice
Consider a 150-employee employer running three locations, a mix of on-site hourly staff and a handful of field employees. The software layer, scheduling, exception management, manager approvals, and payroll sync, runs on Asure Time & Attendance inside AsureCentral. The on-site punches happen on physical clocks through PayClock, delivered through Lathem, an Asure company, with punches syncing directly into Asure Payroll so hours don’t need to be re-keyed. The software subscription is priced against the 150 employees and three-location configuration. The hardware is priced separately, against the number of clocks and the punch method chosen at each site, and that side of the quote comes from Lathem directly.


Treating those as two distinct cost structures, rather than expecting one number to cover both, is what keeps the total cost conversation honest from the start. The software subscription is the ongoing cost of running time and attendance correctly. The hardware is a separate, one-time-per-device decision about how employees interact with the system on site. Getting both pieces right, and getting a real quote for each, is a better foundation for a budget than any single per employee per month figure on its own.
